title: Introduction to Company Accounts
outcomes: Explain what a company is in law and why the company form suits large businesses.
List and explain the salient features of a company, including the present position on the common seal.

Identify the main types of companies under the Companies Act, 2013 (Government, foreign, private, public, OPC, small, listed, unlimited, limited by shares or guarantee, holding and subsidiary) and apply their tests to facts.
State the requirements of section 128 on books of account and section 129 / section 2(40) on financial statements.
Place common items under the correct heads of the Division I, Schedule III balance sheet and statement of profit and loss.

meta.exam_tip: Theory from this unit appears as short notes, true/false with reasons and "distinguish" questions; the Schedule III format is needed in every company-accounts problem that asks for a balance sheet.

concepts.title: Why companies exist, and what "company" means in law
body: Big projects — a steel plant, an airline, a software platform — need more money and more people than a sole trader or a partnership can bring together. The company form lets thousands of investors pool money while professional managers run the business.

The word comes from the Latin "com" (together) and "panis" (bread) — people sharing a meal. In law, a company is one formed and incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, or registered under an earlier company law.

Once incorporated, it is an artificial person: it has its own name, owns property, signs contracts and can sue or be sued. Judges have described it as an artificial being that exists only in the eyes of the law and has perpetual succession.
concepts.analogy: A company is like a cricket franchise: players and owners change every season, but the team keeps its name, its contracts and its trophies.
concepts.work: When a client asks "Should I convert my firm into a company?", a CA explains limited liability, easier fund-raising and continuity — and also the extra compliance (audit, filings, Schedule III accounts) that comes with it.

concepts.title: Salient features of a company
body: Incorporated association — it comes into existence only by registration under the Act. Separate legal entity — it is distinct from its members, so it contracts and is sued in its own name. Perpetual existence — death, insolvency or change of members does not end it.

Common seal — earlier essential for signing documents; it is now optional. Documents that needed the seal may instead be signed by two directors, or by one director and the company secretary. Every company gets a Corporate Identification Number (CIN) from the Registrar of Companies.

Limited liability — a member is liable only for the amount unpaid on his shares; once shares are fully paid, nothing more can be demanded. Ownership is separate from management — shareholders elect a board that runs the business.

Other features — a company is not a citizen (it has legal existence but no citizenship rights); shares are transferable (a private company restricts this); it must keep prescribed books, get them audited periodically by chartered accountants appointed by the shareholders, and give members access to information through meetings and reports (inspection of books beyond what the statute allows is governed by the articles).
concepts.analogy: Limited liability works like a fixed ticket price: once you have paid for your ticket (your shares), the organiser cannot ask you to pay for the stadium's debts.
concepts.work: Bankers and creditors look beyond the promoters to the company's own assets because of the separate-entity rule — which is why they often ask directors for personal guarantees. Explaining this is a routine part of loan advisory work.

concepts.title: Types of companies (1): by control — Government, foreign, holding and subsidiary
body: Government company — s. 2(45): the Central Government, one or more State Governments, or the Centre and the States together own not less than 51% of its paid-up share capital. A subsidiary of a Government company is also a Government company.

Foreign company — s. 2(42): incorporated outside India, having a place of business in India (itself, through an agent, physically or electronically) and carrying on business activity in India in any other manner.

Holding and subsidiary — s. 2(46) and 2(87): Company H is the holding company of S if H controls the composition of S's board of directors (power to appoint or remove most or all of the directors), or exercises or controls more than one-half of S's total share capital, alone or together with its other subsidiaries. Control through another subsidiary (indirect control) also counts. Note: the study material (and the exam) uses "more than one-half of the total share capital"; since 7 May 2018 the Act itself (as amended by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017) reads "more than one-half of the total voting power". For ordinary equity shares carrying one vote each, both tests give the same answer.
concepts.analogy: Holding and subsidiary are like a parent and child on a family plan: the parent decides who is in charge of the child's account.
concepts.work: Group structure decides whether consolidated accounts are needed and which related-party disclosures apply. Auditors map holding–subsidiary chains at the start of every group audit.

concepts.title: Types of companies (2): by public access and size — private, public, OPC, small, listed
body: Private company — s. 2(68): its articles (i) restrict the right to transfer shares, (ii) limit members to 200 (except a One Person Company) — joint holders count as one, and present employees, and former employees who were members while employed and continue as members, are not counted — and (iii) prohibit any invitation to the public to subscribe for its securities. Its shares are not listed.

Public company — s. 2(71): a company that is not a private company. If a private company becomes the subsidiary of a public company, it counts as public for the Act even though its articles still say private. A listed public company that gets delisted remains public. The old minimum paid-up capital (₹1 lakh private, ₹5 lakh public) has been removed.

One Person Company — s. 2(62): only one person as member. Small company — s. 2(85): a company other than a public company whose paid-up capital does not exceed ₹10 crore and whose turnover for the preceding year does not exceed ₹100 crore (as given in the study material); a holding or subsidiary company, a section 8 company or a company under a special Act cannot be a small company.

Listed company — s. 2(52): any of its securities are listed on a recognised stock exchange. A company with no securities listed is unlisted — and an unlisted company may be public or private. So not every public company is listed.
concepts.analogy: A private company is a members-only club with a guest list and no public ticket counter; a listed company sells tickets at the stock exchange window.
concepts.work: Small companies and OPCs enjoy lighter compliance (for example, no cash flow statement). Testing both the capital and the turnover limit every year is a common CA task — crossing either one changes the reporting obligations.

concepts.title: Types of companies (3): by liability — shares, guarantee, unlimited
body: Company limited by shares — s. 2(22): the memorandum caps each member's liability at whatever is still unpaid on his shares. This is the usual form for business companies.

Company limited by guarantee — s. 2(21): members promise in the memorandum to contribute a fixed amount to the company's assets if it is wound up. Common for clubs, chambers of commerce and charitable bodies.
Unlimited company — s. 2(92): no limit on the members' liability.
concepts.analogy: Shares = you pay what is left on your ticket; guarantee = you promise a fixed amount only if the show closes; unlimited = you are on the hook for everything.
concepts.work: In a winding up the liquidator calls on members according to these limits — an auditor or insolvency professional must read the memorandum first.

concepts.title: Maintenance of books of account — section 128
body: For every financial year, every company must maintain books of account, related books and papers and its financial statements, and keep them at its registered office.
They must show a true and fair picture of the company's affairs, branch offices included, and explain transactions at the registered office and branches.
Books must be kept on the accrual basis and under the double entry system. They may be kept in electronic mode as prescribed.
concepts.analogy: The registered office is the company's home address — the law wants its diary (the books) kept at home, whether on paper or on a server.
concepts.work: A company that keeps books on a cash basis breaks section 128 — an auditor would report it. Statutory auditors also check where the books (or their electronic back-up) are kept.

concepts.title: Preparation of financial statements — section 129, section 2(40) and Schedule III
body: Section 129: financial statements must present a true and fair picture, comply with the notified accounting standards and be in the form prescribed in Schedule III. The board lays them before every annual general meeting.

Section 2(40): financial statements include (i) balance sheet at the year end, (ii) profit and loss account (income and expenditure account for a not-for-profit company), (iii) cash flow statement, (iv) statement of changes in equity, if applicable, and (v) explanatory notes. A One Person Company, small company and dormant company may omit the cash flow statement.

Insurance, banking and electricity companies, and any class for which another Act prescribes a format, follow that Act. All others follow Schedule III: Division I — companies applying the notified Accounting Standards; Division II — companies applying Ind AS; Division III — NBFCs applying Ind AS. Each division has Part I (balance sheet) and Part II (statement of profit and loss). Foundation uses Division I.
concepts.analogy: Schedule III is a standard exam answer sheet: everyone writes in the same boxes, so the examiner (investor) can compare answers quickly.
concepts.work: Converting a trial balance into Schedule III statements — grouping ledgers, splitting current and non-current, writing notes — is the core of year-end finalisation work in any CA firm.

concepts.title: The Division I balance sheet and statement of profit and loss
body: Balance sheet, Equity and Liabilities side: 1. Shareholders' funds — share capital, reserves and surplus, money received against share warrants; 2. Share application money pending allotment; 3. Non-current liabilities — long-term borrowings, deferred tax liabilities (net), other long-term liabilities, long-term provisions; 4. Current liabilities — short-term borrowings, trade payables (MSE dues shown separately), other current liabilities, short-term provisions.

Assets side: 1. Non-current assets — property, plant and equipment and intangible assets (PPE, intangible assets, capital work-in-progress, intangible assets under development), non-current investments, deferred tax assets (net), long-term loans and advances, other non-current assets; 2. Current assets — current investments, inventories, trade receivables, cash and cash equivalents, short-term loans and advances, other current assets.

Share capital note shows, for each class: shares authorised; issued, subscribed and fully paid / not fully paid; par value; reconciliation of shares at the start and end of the year; calls unpaid; forfeited shares. Only paid-up capital enters the total. Reserves and surplus sub-heads include capital reserve, capital redemption reserve, securities premium, debenture redemption reserve, revaluation reserve, share options outstanding, surplus and other reserves.

Statement of profit and loss: Revenue from operations + Other income = Total income; less expenses (materials consumed, purchases of stock-in-trade, changes in inventories, employee benefits, finance costs, depreciation and amortisation, other expenses); then exceptional and extraordinary items, tax, profit from continuing and discontinuing operations, and basic and diluted earnings per share.

concepts.work: Misclassifying the current portion of a term loan as non-current makes liquidity ratios look better than they are — lenders and auditors check this split carefully.

jobs.title: First finalisation: grouping a trial balance into Schedule III
jobs.role: Articled assistant in a CA firm (accounts finalisation of a manufacturing company)
jobs.situation: Your manager hands you the trial balance of a private company and asks for a draft Schedule III balance sheet. The ledger has a "Term loan — HDFC" of ₹30 lakh, of which ₹6 lakh is repayable in the next 12 months, a "Calls in arrears" balance and an "Unpaid dividend" account.
steps: Map each ledger to a Schedule III head and sub-head; keep a mapping sheet so it can be reviewed.
Split the term loan: ₹24 lakh under long-term borrowings, ₹6 lakh as current maturities of long-term borrowings under short-term borrowings.
Deduct calls in arrears from called-up capital inside the share capital note — do not show it as an asset.
Show unpaid dividend under other current liabilities.
Check that the share capital note gives authorised, issued, subscribed, called-up and paid-up figures and the reconciliation of number of shares.
jobs.takeaway: Schedule III is not just a format — the current/non-current split and the notes change how lenders and investors read the company.
jobs.think: Why is calls in arrears not shown as a current asset (a receivable)?
jobs.answer: Because it is capital that was called but never received; Schedule III requires paid-up capital to be shown, so unpaid calls are deducted from called-up capital.

jobs.title: Advising a founder on the right type of company
jobs.role: Practising CA advising a start-up founder
jobs.situation: A founder plans to start alone, later bring in 10 friends as investors, and perhaps list in 8 years. She asks whether to form an OPC, a private company or a public company.
steps: Explain an OPC: one member, lighter compliance, but it must convert if more members join.
Explain a private company: up to 200 members, share transfers restricted, no public invitation — suits friends-and-family funding.
Explain a public company and listing: needed to raise money from the public; heavier compliance and disclosure.
Point out that a private company can later convert into a public company before an IPO.
Mention small-company relief while capital and turnover stay within the limits.
jobs.takeaway: The type of company drives compliance cost, fund-raising options and even the format of financial statements.
jobs.think: If the founder's private company becomes a subsidiary of a public company, what is its status?
jobs.answer: It is deemed to be a public company under the proviso to s. 2(71), even if its articles still call it private.

mcqs.q: A company in which the Central Government holds 26% and two State Governments together hold 27% of the paid-up share capital is:
options: Not a Government company, because no single government holds 51%
mcqs.explain: Under section 2(45) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company is a Government company if the Central Government, one or more State Governments, or the Centre and States together hold at least 51% of its paid-up share capital. Here 26% + 27% = 53%, so it qualifies. The trap is thinking one government alone must hold 51% — holdings are added together. In practice: many joint Centre–State undertakings, such as some metro rail corporations, are Government companies on this combined basis.

mcqs.q: A company incorporated in Singapore that has an office in Chennai and does business in India is:
mcqs.explain: Section 2(42) defines a foreign company as one incorporated outside India that has a place of business in India (directly, through an agent, physically or electronically) and carries on business activity in India. A Singapore company with a Chennai office doing business here fits exactly. The trap is 'subsidiary company', which depends on control by a holding company, not on place of incorporation. In practice: foreign companies with Indian branch offices must file their accounts with the Registrar every year.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a condition in the articles of a private company?
options: It may invite the public to subscribe for its shares
It restricts the right to transfer its shares
It limits its members to 200 (except an OPC)
It prohibits invitation to the public to subscribe for securities
mcqs.explain: Under section 2(68), a private company's articles must restrict the right to transfer shares, limit members to 200 (except for an OPC) and prohibit any invitation to the public to subscribe for its securities. So 'it may invite the public to subscribe' is not a condition — it is exactly what a private company cannot do. The trap is the 200-member limit, which looks like a size rule but is a genuine condition. In practice: start-ups raise funds from angel investors through private placement, never public offers.

options: An unlisted company may be either public or private
Every public company is a listed company
A private company can list its equity shares
A listed company that is delisted becomes a private company
mcqs.explain: A listed company has securities listed on a recognised stock exchange. Many public companies are unlisted, and every private company is unlisted, so an unlisted company may be either public or private. The trap 'every public company is listed' is wrong — listing is optional for public companies. A delisted public company remains public; it does not become private automatically. In practice: many large unlisted public companies, such as some infrastructure firms, raise funds through privately placed debentures.

mcqs.q: A private company (not part of any group) has paid-up capital of ₹8 crore and turnover of ₹105 crore. As per the limits in the study material it is:
options: Not a small company, because turnover exceeds ₹100 crore
A small company, because paid-up capital is within ₹10 crore
A small company, because it is private
mcqs.explain: Under section 2(85) and the limits in the study material, a small company must satisfy both conditions: paid-up capital not exceeding ₹10 crore and turnover not exceeding ₹100 crore (and not be a holding or subsidiary company). Capital of ₹8 crore passes, but turnover of ₹105 crore fails, so it is not a small company. The trap is treating either condition alone as sufficient. In practice: small companies get relief such as omitting the cash flow statement and fewer board meetings.

mcqs.q: Books of account of a company must be kept at:
options: The office of its statutory auditor
The residence of the managing director
mcqs.explain: Section 128 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires books of account to be kept at the company's registered office, though the board may decide to keep them at another place in India, and they may be kept electronically. The trap is the auditor's office — the auditor examines books but does not hold them. In practice: companies using cloud ERP must ensure the server back-up and access remain available in India as required under the rules.

mcqs.q: Under section 128, books of account must be maintained on:
options: Accrual basis under the double entry system
Cash basis under the double entry system
Cash or accrual basis, as the board decides
Single entry, if the company is small
mcqs.explain: Section 128 requires every company to keep books of account on an accrual basis and according to the double entry system. Neither cash basis nor single entry is allowed, whatever the company's size. The trap 'cash or accrual, as the board decides' would let companies choose cash accounting, which the Act does not permit. In practice: even a small private company with modest turnover must book outstanding expenses and accrued income at year-end.

mcqs.q: Which companies may omit the cash flow statement from their financial statements?
options: One Person Company, small company and dormant company
mcqs.explain: The proviso to section 2(40) allows a One Person Company, a small company and a dormant company to omit the cash flow statement from their financial statements. The trap 'all private companies' is wrong — only private companies that also qualify as small companies (or OPCs) get the relief. In practice: an auditor checks whether a private client truly meets the small-company limits before accepting accounts without a cash flow statement.

mcqs.q: Division II of Schedule III applies to:
options: Companies required to follow Ind AS (other than NBFCs)
Companies following the notified Accounting Standards
mcqs.explain: Schedule III has three divisions: Division I for companies following the notified Accounting Standards, Division II for companies required to follow Ind AS (other than NBFCs), and Division III for NBFCs following Ind AS. The trap is 'companies following Accounting Standards', which is Division I. In practice: listed companies and large unlisted ones above Ind AS thresholds present their balance sheets in the Division II format.

mcqs.q: Called-up capital ₹9,00,000; calls unpaid ₹12,000. The share capital shown in the balance sheet total is:
mcqs.explain: Called-up capital is the amount the company has asked shareholders to pay. Calls unpaid (calls in arrears) are deducted to get paid-up capital: 9,00,000 − 12,000 = ₹8,88,000, shown in the balance sheet total. The trap ₹9,00,000 shows called-up capital and ignores the unpaid calls. In practice: the notes to accounts show issued, subscribed and called-up capital with calls unpaid deducted, as required by Schedule III.

mcqs.q: Securities premium is shown in the balance sheet under:
mcqs.explain: Securities premium is the excess of the issue price over the face value of shares. It is not share capital, so it is shown under Shareholders' funds — Reserves and surplus, as a separate item. The trap 'share capital' would overstate the face-value capital. In practice: when a listed company issues shares at a premium, the premium is credited to Securities Premium and can be used only for purposes allowed by section 52, such as issuing bonus shares.

mcqs.q: Use of the common seal under the Companies Act today is:
options: Optional; documents may be signed by two directors or a director and the company secretary
Abolished, and no company may have a seal
mcqs.explain: Since the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2015, a common seal is optional. Where a document needs authentication, two directors, or one director and the company secretary, may sign it instead. The trap 'compulsory on every document' reflects the old position before 2015. In practice: many companies no longer have seals; banks and registries accept board resolutions and authorised signatures.

questions.q: Explain any five salient features of a company.

items: Incorporated association: a company exists only after registration under the Companies Act, 2013; it is an artificial legal person created by law.
Separate legal entity: it is distinct from its members, so it owns property, makes contracts and sues or is sued in its own name.
Perpetual existence: death, insolvency or change of members does not affect its existence.
Limited liability: a member's liability is limited to the amount unpaid on his shares; fully paid shares carry no further liability.
Separation of ownership and management: shareholders elect a board of directors which manages the company.

Also acceptable: common seal (now optional — two directors or a director and CS may sign), transferability of shares (restricted in a private company), statutory books, periodic audit, right of access to information, not a citizen.

remarks: Half a mark is lost when a feature is only named — each needs one line of explanation.
Many candidates still write that the common seal is compulsory; the current position is that it is optional.
mistakes: Saying a private company's shares are freely transferable.
Writing the same point twice under two headings (separate entity and perpetual existence are different features).
tips: Use a bold heading for each feature followed by one or two lines.
Write exactly the number asked; extra points earn nothing but take time.

viva.q: What is a company? Explain its meaning in law.
viva.model: In law, a company is an association of persons formed and incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, or under an earlier company law. Once incorporated it becomes an artificial person with a separate legal entity, distinct from its members. It has perpetual succession, so its existence is not affected when members die or change, and it acts through a board of directors elected by the shareholders.

points.pt: Formed and incorporated (registered) under the Companies Act, 2013 or an earlier company law
An artificial (legal) person — separate legal entity distinct from its members
Perpetual succession — not affected by death or change of members

viva.q: Define a Government company under the Companies Act, 2013.
viva.model: Under section 2(45), a Government company is one where at least fifty-one per cent of its paid-up share capital is owned by the Central Government, by one or more State Governments, or by the Central and State Governments together. A subsidiary of such a Government company is also a Government company.

viva.q: What are the three restrictions that a private company must place in its articles?
viva.model: A private company must, by its articles, first restrict the right to transfer its shares; second, limit its members to two hundred, except in a One Person Company, not counting present and past employees who are members; and third, prohibit any invitation to the public to subscribe for its securities.

viva.q: What does section 128 require about the books of account of a company?
viva.model: Section 128 requires every company to prepare and keep books of account for every financial year at its registered office. The books must show a true and fair picture of the company's affairs, including branches, and must be kept on the accrual basis and according to the double entry system. They may also be kept in electronic mode.

viva.q: What do financial statements include under section 2(40), and which companies may leave out the cash flow statement?
viva.model: Under section 2(40), financial statements include a balance sheet at the end of the year, a profit and loss account or an income and expenditure account, a cash flow statement, a statement of changes in equity if applicable, and explanatory notes. A One Person Company, a small company and a dormant company may leave out the cash flow statement.

cases.title: Sarthak Agro — choosing and presenting
cases.case: Sarthak Agro Pvt Ltd was incorporated in 2024. Its articles restrict share transfers and bar any public invitation for securities. It has 140 members, of whom 25 are employees. Its paid-up capital is ₹3 crore and its turnover for 2025-26 was ₹42 crore; it is not a holding or subsidiary company. On 31 March 2027 its ledger shows, among others: 20,000 equity shares of ₹100 each, ₹80 called up; calls unpaid on 600 shares at ₹30 per share; securities premium ₹1,50,000; and 9% debentures of ₹5,00,000 repayable in 2032.

mcqs.q: Which description fits Sarthak Agro Pvt Ltd for 2026-27?
options: A private company that is also a small company
A public company because it has more than 50 members
mcqs.explain: Sarthak meets all three conditions of a private company: restricted share transfers, no public invitation and members within 200 (140). It is also a small company under the limits in the study material: paid-up capital ₹3 crore (≤ ₹10 crore), turnover ₹42 crore (≤ ₹100 crore), and it is neither a holding nor subsidiary. The trap 'public because more than 50 members' uses the old pre-2013 limit. In practice: being small gives Sarthak lighter compliance.

mcqs.q: What paid-up share capital will appear on the face of the balance sheet?
mcqs.explain: Called-up capital = 20,000 × ₹80 = ₹16,00,000. Calls unpaid = 600 × ₹30 = ₹18,000. Paid-up capital = 16,00,000 − 18,000 = ₹15,82,000. The trap ₹16,00,000 ignores calls unpaid; ₹20,00,000 is the nominal value of shares issued, not the called-up amount. In practice: the company's notes to accounts show issued, subscribed, called-up and paid-up capital step by step as required by Schedule III.

mcqs.q: Under which head will the 9% debentures appear?
mcqs.explain: Debentures repayable after more than 12 months from the balance sheet date are long-term borrowings, shown under Non-current liabilities. These 9% debentures are repayable in 2032, so they appear under Long-term borrowings (bonds/debentures). The trap 'share capital' confuses borrowed funds with ownership funds. In practice: the portion of debentures falling due within the next 12 months is reclassified as current maturities under Other current liabilities.

mcqs.q: Which statement may Sarthak Agro leave out of its financial statements?
options: The statement of profit and loss
mcqs.explain: The proviso to section 2(40) allows a small company to omit the cash flow statement. Sarthak qualifies as small, so it may leave out the cash flow statement, but must still prepare the balance sheet, statement of profit and loss and notes. The trap 'notes to accounts' is wrong — notes are an integral part of the financial statements. In practice: auditors confirm small-company status every year, since crossing the limits brings back the cash flow requirement.

summary: A company is incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 (or earlier law): an artificial person, separate from its members, with perpetual succession.

Features: incorporated association, separate entity, perpetual existence, common seal (optional now), limited liability, ownership separate from management, not a citizen, transferable shares, statutory books, periodic audit, access to information.

Types: Government (≥51% paid-up capital with governments), foreign, private (restrict transfer, ≤200 members, no public invitation), public, OPC, small (₹10 crore capital and ₹100 crore turnover as per material), listed, unlimited, limited by shares or guarantee, holding and subsidiary (board control or > ½ total share capital).
Section 128: books at registered office, true and fair, accrual basis, double entry; electronic mode allowed.
Section 129 + 2(40): balance sheet, P&L, cash flow (not needed for OPC/small/dormant), SOCE if applicable, notes; formats in Schedule III Division I/II/III.
remember: Only paid-up capital enters the balance sheet total; authorised, issued and subscribed are disclosed in the note.
Calls unpaid are deducted from called-up capital.
Securities premium, CRR, DRR, capital reserve, revaluation reserve → Reserves and surplus.
Share application money pending allotment is a separate head between shareholders' funds and non-current liabilities.
traps: Not every public company is listed.
Government holdings — Central and State — are added for the 51% test.
Small company needs BOTH limits; a public, holding or subsidiary company can never be small.
The common seal is optional, not compulsory.
